title: Death by reimbursement cut
dek: Medicare trims rates every year while labor costs rise — providers and device makers watch margins collapse even as volume grows.
lede: The story of US healthcare providers in 2025-2026 is a squeeze you can measure in basis points. Medicare keeps cutting. Inflation keeps rising. Volume ticks up because America is aging and getting sicker, but the price per treatment falls year after year. Only the biggest players with the scale to absorb the cuts survive.
what_changed:
Start with dialysis. In 2025, 516,837 Americans were on dialysis—a number that will keep rising because the US population is aging and diabetes is endemic. The market is $36 billion today, projected to reach $37.7 billion by 2026, a healthy-sounding 3.5% annual growth. But here's the trap: Medicare rate increases for 2026 are 2.2%. For 2027, they drop to 1.1%. These are the official numbers from CMS. Dialysis labor costs—wages for nurses, techs, and clinic managers—are running 3-5% annually. So every year the gap widens. Dialysis clinics are now at 11.7% operating margins for the strongest players like Fresenius (Q2 2026), and that's only by squeezing harder: cutting costs, shifting mix toward higher-acuity premium services like hemodiafiltration, and pushing patients toward home dialysis (now 17.4% of the dialysis population in 2022, up from 10% in 2016). The two giants—DaVita at 38% market share and Fresenius at 27%—have the scale to invest in new technologies like Fresenius's 5008X system (deployed in 227 US clinics by Q2 2026) and DaVita's high-efficiency dialyzer programs. Smaller independent dialysis operators don't. They're getting picked off or absorbed by regional PE roll-ups that bet on operational excellence to survive the margin grind.

The same structural trap plays out in ambulatory surgery centers, which is a $46.5 billion market growing at 6.3% year-over-year. That sounds like expansion—and volume-wise it is, because America's aging population needs more procedures. But reimbursement is growing at 2.4-2.9% annually. Wage inflation and operational cost increases are running 3-5%. The result is a bifurcation: large, integrated platforms like USPI maintain 38.6% EBITDA margins in 2025 by absorbing smaller independent ASCs into consolidated operations. Smaller independents, which make up 67% of the 6,500+ Medicare-certified ASCs in the US, are being squeezed to the low-to-mid 30s. Ascension Health's $3.9 billion acquisition of AmSurg (2024), expanding from 58 to 300+ centers across 34 states, is the playbook: buy independents, consolidate overhead, enforce standardized protocols, and negotiate better supply contracts. CMS added 560 new procedures to the ASC Covered Procedures List in 2026—cardiac ablations, lumbar fusion, and others—but these high-acuity procedures carry thinner margins at ASCs than at hospital outpatient departments because site-of-service payment differentials are baked in. The scale players can afford to absorb the thinner margins on a few procedures if it means filling the OR schedule and spreading fixed costs. Smaller operators can't.

Diagnostic imaging is the starkest case of reimbursement collapse. The market is $26.3 billion in 2026, growing at just 1.7% CAGR since 2021. Medicare's conversion factor dropped 2.83% in 2025 alone. Since 2003, MRI reimbursement has fallen 76.5%. CT imaging has fallen 69.1%. These are cumulative declines over two decades, and they're baked into current payment. Imaging centers are at 17-18% margins, below where they need to be to reinvest in AI and infrastructure. Radiologist shortages are acute: 961 diagnostic radiology residency applicants went unmatched in 2025. It takes 130 days to fill a radiology position. Hospitals hold 41.5% of outpatient imaging claims and are capturing share from freestanding centers. Radiology Partners, one of the largest independent imaging networks, had to raise $720 million in fresh equity in February 2026 just to reduce debt—a sign of financial distress. Private equity is consolidating the market aggressively (13 acquisitions in 2025), betting that AI automation and platform scale can restore margins. But smaller independent imaging centers—the ones without PE backing or hospital integration—are being pushed out.

What does this force make scarce, cheap, risky, and valuable? It makes small-scale independent providers risky. It makes operational excellence valuable—the ability to cut cost without cutting quality. It makes labor cheap in the sense that providers are forced to compete harder for talent on wage suppression, which means flooded job markets in some geographies and chronic shortages in others. It makes scale a moat: the bigger you are, the more leverage you have to negotiate with suppliers, to spread fixed costs like IT and compliance across more revenue, and to absorb year-over-year margin compression. It makes consolidation valuable—every major player we see (DaVita, Fresenius, USPI, Ascension, Surgery Partners, Radiology Partners) is either acquiring competitors or raising capital to do so. And it makes innovation in the specific direction of operational efficiency—AI-driven diagnostics, high-volume modalities like hemodiafiltration, automated home-based systems—the only viable path to recovery.

A third risk is geographic access: rural and lower-income urban markets are the least profitable for dialysis, ASCs, and imaging. If only the big platforms survive, coverage will concentrate in higher-income, higher-payer-mix geographies, leaving entire regions without accessible services."
one_sentence: Medicare cuts compound every year while labor costs rise, forcing independent providers into a choice between consolidation, collapse, or radical cost cuts that hollow out the middle market.

title: The specialist squeeze
dek: Medicare cuts and administrative burden push solo practitioners into consolidation and PE deals.
lede: Specialists used to own their practices. Not anymore. Medicare reimbursement cuts, rising overhead, and the sheer weight of billing compliance have made solo practice unsustainable. Cardiologists, dermatologists, and OB-GYNs are getting absorbed into hospital systems and private equity platforms—not because they want scale, but because they can't survive alone.
what_changed:
Medicare's squeeze on procedure pricing is relentless and specific. Cardiologists saw their reimbursement fall 29% from 2005 to 2021 while hospital payments rose 70%—a 99-point gap that tells you everything about where the money goes. Then in 2026, the CMS took a sledgehammer: stress tests dropped from $311.40 to $220.60 per procedure, amyloid PET imaging was slashed 57%, and left atrial appendage closures—critical for heart failure patients—lost 27% in work value. A cardiologist doing 20 stress tests a month just lost $1,820 in gross revenue overnight. Dermatologists are watching a 9% reimbursement cut proposed for 2027, even as they're still heavily dependent on Medicare (though they're hedging by expanding cosmetic practices, where margins hit 30-50% instead of 10-15%). OB-GYNs face a different squeeze: birth rates hit an all-time low of 1.6 children per woman in 2026 (3.6 million births, down 1% from 2024), which means fewer obstetric cases, but they're also stuck in abortion-ban states where Idaho alone lost 35% of its OB-GYN workforce between mid-2022 and end-2024. Residency applications to ban states dropped 6.7% in 2024 while applications to abortion-legal states barely budged at 0.4% growth. The result: fewer physicians in high-restriction states doing fewer deliveries, while those who remain face expanded liability and regulatory uncertainty.

The cost side of the equation is moving just as fast. Private practice economics are no longer viable. The cardiology industry has compressed from 240,000 establishments in 2021 to 165,000 in 2025 as consolidation accelerates; 90% of cardiologists now work for hospitals or PE-backed groups instead of running their own shops. Dermatology is 85% fragmented (12,000 dermatologists in 6,000 establishments), but 35+ PE-backed multi-state platforms are swallowing independent practices at record pace—16 buyout deals completed through October 2025, with multiples at 3-5x EBITDA for solo practices and 4-9x for small groups. The draw isn't prestige or scale efficiency; it's survival. EMR mandates, compliance complexity, and rising staff costs are eating into margins that Medicare cuts have already shrunk. A solo cardiologist used to earn a 13.9% net margin (2025 baseline); that's before paying for the new AI workload and the administrative staff it now takes to track 7,700 procedural codes that CMS changed in one rule drop.

Technology is adding a strange wrinkle. Remote patient monitoring in cardiology grew to $4.68 billion in 2025, and 87% of physicians said telehealth adoption will keep rising. AI-enabled ECG interpretation and DermaSensor (FDA-approved in 2024 for melanoma detection in primary care) are shifting diagnostic work to non-specialists. That's volume erosion for specialists who relied on referral streams—a cardiologist's patient population can now be partially managed remotely or screened by a primary-care doctor with an AI tool. Meanwhile, cardiologist shortage is severe: the ratio will deteriorate from 1 per 1,087 patients (2025) to 1 per 1,700 patients (2035), with 547 cardiologists retiring annually by 2031. Burnout is real. None of this is getting better.

The only path forward for most specialists is consolidation. Hospital systems now employ 47% of OB-GYNs (2024), up from a fragmented private-practice model a decade ago. PE platforms in dermatology saw dermatologists gain 3-5% reimbursement improvements within 18 months of acquisition—not from new prices, but from operational leverage and coding optimization. Cardiologists have already made the move: H1 2025 saw six PE acquisitions in cardiology, matching the entire 2024 volume. They're also expanding adjacent services—cosmetic dermatology margins are so much fatter (12.4% CAGR growth in the medical aesthetics market, global market jumped from $19.55B in 2025 to $22.59B in 2026) that dermatologists are pouring investment into lasers and injectables as insurance against Medicare. For OB-GYNs, the pathway is into health systems that can absorb malpractice liability, hire midwives to fill obstetric slots, and diversify revenue into preventive care and contraception—which is booming even as births crash.

win: Hospitals and PE-backed platforms win. Hospitals gain physician employment (47% of OB-GYNs in 2024), liability insurance bundled with the health system, and the ability to absorb reimbursement cuts through operational leverage. PE platforms in dermatology see acquisitions yield 3-5% reimbursement gains within 18 months post-close through coding optimization and billing at scale. Larger groups can hire compliance staff, negotiate EMR contracts as a bloc, and diversify revenue streams—cardiologists adding remote monitoring ($4.68B market in 2025), dermatologists expanding cosmetic services (12.4% CAGR growth). The big platforms also have capital to invest in AI and technology—AI-enabled ECG interpretation, DermaSensor for primary-care melanoma screening—that shifts routine work down the chain or automates it away, preserving profits on the high-value cases that only specialists do.
lose: Solo and small-group specialists get squeezed. Cardiologists going it alone can no longer absorb $91/procedure cuts on stress tests (a routine revenue item) or 57% slashes on imaging. Dermatologists face a 9% Medicare cut in 2027 while their solo-practice economics deteriorate. OB-GYNs in abortion-ban states are fleeing—Idaho's 35% exodus is just the visible part; smaller state-level losses add up. Even as they're forced into consolidation, specialists surrender autonomy, accept lower profit-share agreements with PE buyers (working for PE at lower take-home rate but with the platform's compliance and billing infrastructure), and face volume compression from AI-assisted primary-care screening and telehealth. Birth volume is collapsing (1.6 fertility rate, 3.6M births), cardiologist supply is shrinking relative to an aging population that needs more care, and dermatologists are competing for a fixed pool of Medicare referrals. The solo specialist model is functionally extinct.
worry: The biggest risk is that consolidation simply passes Medicare cuts down the line without improving outcomes. A PE platform acquires 20 solo dermatology practices, rolls them into one billing system, and gains 3-5% efficiency on the margins—but that gain is temporary. The 9% reimbursement cut in 2027 erases those gains within months, and the PE owner either forces volume expansion (which hits saturation) or cuts corners on care. For cardiologists, the math is brutal: 547 retiring annually by 2031, 1 cardiologist per 1,700 patients by 2035, and an aging population with rising heart disease prevalence (41.9% obesity, 7.7 million heart failure cases). There aren't enough cardiologists to go around, yet reimbursement keeps falling. Remote monitoring and AI screening may take some load off, but they're not a replacement for interventional procedures or complex diagnosis—and those are exactly the procedures Medicare is cutting. For OB-GYNs, the risk is geographic collapse of obstetric capacity in ban states. If 35% of physicians flee, residency slots empty, and births decline further, rural obstetrics disappears—and then abortion-legal states become the only places with robust maternity capacity, forcing patients to travel or forcing births to happen with inadequate care. The system isn't rebalancing toward better efficiency; it's fracturing.
one_sentence: Medicare cuts and administrative burden have made solo specialist practice uneconomical, forcing consolidation into hospitals and PE platforms that gain efficiency but may simply extract value without solving the underlying shortage of specialists.

title: The device price grind
dek: Device makers face 1-2% annual price cuts as Medicare freezes reimbursement and hospitals consolidate their buying power.
lede: Device makers built their business on the assumption that an aging population means growing prices. It turns out they only got half the deal. Yes, volume is rising—more hip replacements, more dialysis, more surgical robots. But the price per unit keeps falling, year after year, and there's nowhere to hide.
what_changed:
The orthopedic device market is the clearest case. US orthopedic products manufacturing was a $60.6 billion market in 2025, growing at 4.3% annually through 2035, which sounds healthy until you look at the numbers behind it. Margins sit at 5.6%—squeezed down from higher levels just a few years ago. Medicare reimbursement for hip replacements fell 39% since 2017. For standard knee replacements, reimbursement dropped 26% from 2016 to 2024. In January 2026, CMS added a 2.5% efficiency adjustment on top. Hospitals are consolidating their purchasing power at the same time device makers are consolidating their companies. When you're one of 480 establishments competing for contracts from a shrinking number of hospital systems, you have nowhere to go but down on price. Stryker took the MAKO robotic knee surgery platform and made it the standard of care—67% of US knee procedures and 33% of hip procedures ran on MAKO by end of 2025. But even dominance doesn't save you. The price pressure is structural. J&J spun out DePuy Synthes, a $20 billion orthopedic business, signaling that even the giants don't want to be trapped in that margin grind anymore.

Dialysis equipment tells the same story with a twist—the volume is there but the reimbursement isn't following. The US dialysis equipment market hit $14.3 billion in 2025 and is growing at 4.8% to 5.2% annually, but margins are just 5–6%, well below the medical device industry average of 12%. Manufacturers face a double squeeze. First, Medicare: the 2026 ESRD base rate rose to $281.71, only 2.2% higher than the year before—far below inflation—so clinics are deferring equipment purchases and pushing that pain onto makers. Second, tariffs are now a material cost. US duties on medical devices from China hit 25–54% in 2025, and when Mexico imposed 35–50% tariffs on Chinese goods starting in January 2026, the cost of components spiked. Baxter sold its entire kidney care business to Carlyle in January 2025 for $3.8 billion, signaling retreat. Even Fresenius, the market leader, is acting defensive—it spent EUR 312 million in September 2025 just to buy out the remaining non-physician stakes in Interwell Health, tightening control over the supply chain because the alternative is losing margin on every unit sold. The one bright spot for device makers is portable and implantable kidney technology in trials, but that's years away. For now, the business is volume with a falling price tag.

The entire medical device sector faces a restructuring that favors only the largest players. The US medical device manufacturing industry generated $59.4 billion in 2026, growing just 2.4% year over year, with EBIT margins around 12–12.4% under pressure from tariffs and labor costs. A 10% global tariff hit in April 2025, and syringes and needles faced tariffs of 50–100%. J&J alone warned of $400 million in added costs for 2025. Abbott warned of hundreds of millions more. The FDA's new Quality Management System Regulation took effect February 2, 2026, requiring tighter supplier controls and traceability—compliance overhead that only large companies can absorb. The result: $36.5 billion in medtech M&A in the first half of 2026, with consolidation accelerating. The 1,067 establishment players in the industry are shrinking. The top 10 OEMs are buying up smaller innovators, not to grow share but to secure patents and consolidate the cost burden. Scale is the only defense. A company with $60 billion in revenue can absorb tariff shock, FDA compliance, and 1–2% annual price cuts. A company with $500 million in revenue cannot.

What did this force make scarce, cheap, risky, and valuable? It made pricing power vanishingly scarce. It made volume cheap—the orthopedic market grew 4.3% annually, but price-per-unit fell 1–2% every year, so real revenue growth came from doing more procedures for less money. It made remaining independent risky—if you're a mid-size device maker, you're either being squeezed out of contracts by larger competitors or forced to compete on price alone. And it made scale newly valuable. Companies with global supply chains, tariff-resilient sourcing, and compliance infrastructure at scale are winning. Smaller players are being acquired or shuttered.

But even Stryker is not immune to the margin grind. The real winners are hospital systems and payers, who are consolidating and using their scale to demand 1–2% price cuts year after year.
lose: Mid-size and independent device makers are being squeezed out. If you have $500 million to $2 billion in annual revenue, you can't absorb tariff shocks the way Medtronic can. You can't spread FDA compliance costs across 50,000 SKUs. You can't negotiate favorable tariff treatment because you don't have the lobbying power of the giants. You end up being acquired at a discount, or you exit the market. Baxter exiting kidney care is the signal. J&J spinning out DePuy Synthes is the same message in a different package. For smaller orthopedic innovators, the choice is to be bought by Stryker, Zimmer Biomet, or whoever else, or watch your margins compress 1–2% a year until you're no longer viable.
worry: The single biggest risk is that pricing power doesn't come back. Device makers are betting that once tariff chaos settles or inflation slows, they can raise prices again. They are probably wrong. Medicare reimbursement is set by law, and Congress is not going to vote to pay more for hip replacements. Hospital systems are consolidating and getting more skilled at driving prices down. The aging population keeps getting older, which means volume is still growing, but volume without pricing power is a race to the bottom. If you're a device maker in 2026, you're making more units for less money, and the only way to stay profitable is to get bigger, cut costs more aggressively than your competitors, or exit segments where scale is no longer defensible. That sounds survivable until you realize that tariff costs, labor costs, and compliance costs are all going up in absolute terms even if volume is growing.
one_sentence: Device makers are being forced to choose between scale or exit—there is no middle ground left.

title: Generic-Drug Deflation
dek: Medicare-driven price cuts and PBM dominance compress margins and force smaller makers out of commodity generics.
lede: The generic drug market in the US went from $40.6 billion in 2022 to $28.5 billion by 2026—a 30% collapse in four years. This isn't a demand crisis; Americans are taking more pills than ever as the population ages. The price per pill just keeps falling. PBMs now control 80% of what gets paid, and federal regulators are finally cracking down on their markups, but that regulatory whip doesn't help manufacturers. It tightens the screws even harder.
what_changed:
The generic drug business became two industries in 2026. One is the commodity trap: pills that cost a few cents to make and get squeezed down to fractions of a cent by massive buyers. PBMs—pharmacy benefit managers like Caremark, Express Scripts, and OptumRx—hold the whip. They decide which drugs insurers will cover and at what price, and they pocket the spread between what they pay manufacturers and what they charge employers. The FTC documented how these three companies exploit that gap on specialty generics. By February 2026, Congress had had enough and passed legislation to delink PBM compensation from drug prices, forcing them onto flat service fees instead. That was a landmark moment. But it doesn't raise generic drug prices for manufacturers. It just kills one revenue stream for PBMs without giving manufacturers back their margin.

The other industry is the escape route: complex generics, biosimilars, and first-to-market plays where price compression moves slower. Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers—429 businesses in 2025, down 2.4% annually since 2021—face a simple math problem. Margins on commodity generics collapsed to 5–15%, sometimes lower when a dozen makers chase the same 500-tablet bottle. Branded generics (reformulations, new dosages, combination therapies) still hold 20–40% margins, and biosimilars, in their early years, command higher prices before competition arrives. Teva, the world's largest generic maker, reported 15% US generics growth in 2024 but gave subdued guidance for 2025, a public signal that the commodity game is ending. Sandoz, the generics arm of Novartis, launched three biosimilars in Europe in late 2025 (Afqlir, Jubbonti, Wyost) and signaled it would target mid-to-high single-digit growth through biosimilar expansion in 2026—a frank admission that commodity generics are not a growth business anymore.

The global supply chain is now a second pressure valve. India ships $10.5 billion in pharmaceutical goods to the US annually and depends on China for 70% of raw materials. These imports now account for 58% of US pharmaceutical imports by weight. That abundance keeps commodity generic prices international lows, but it also means any US manufacturer trying to compete on volume will get outbid by players who can run factories in Hyderabad for pennies on the dollar. The Trump administration has signaled 100% tariffs on generic drugs by August 2028, and Congress has advanced the PILLS Act to incentivize US-based manufacturing with subsidies. Both moves are explicit economic warfare against the import-dependent commodity generic model—a signal that the political consensus has shifted. But tariffs don't arrive until 2028, and by then the structural winners (scale players like Teva, Sandoz, and Aurobindo) will have already pivoted away. The FDA, under GDUFA III through September 2027, is accelerating generic approvals—87 new first-time generics approved in 2025—which floods the market with new competitors the day any therapy loses patent protection. That's exactly backward for a compressed-margin business.

What this force made cheap: generic pills themselves—fractions of a cent each. It made risky the business of making commodity generics in the US; the cost of goods is no longer the binding constraint, and regulatory scrutiny, tariff uncertainty, and PBM price-setting are. It made scarce the old profit model of mid-sized generics makers who relied on market share volume. And it made newly valuable the ability to own a portfolio of complex, difficult-to-copy therapeutics—biosimilars, niche molecules, specialty formulations—where a single manufacturer can retain pricing power across a multi-year period before the next maker catches up.

By then, the consolidation will be done. PBMs lose their most profitable revenue stream once the February 2026 legislation takes full effect and flat-fee compensation replaces the price-spread arbitrage—but that's a redistribution to insurers and employers, not to manufacturers, so it's a win for payers, not a win for the people making pills.
worry: The single biggest risk is a structural orphaning of scarce, older generics that don't have scale economics. If a small manufacturer is the only maker of a 30-year-old drug and can't compete on price with imports, it will exit, and supply can tighten. Generic shortages in oncology, antibiotics, and cardiac drugs have already snarled US hospitals multiple times. The FDA is aware and is pushing manufacturers to secure supply chains before tariffs arrive, but the incentive structure is broken: a manufacturer facing 5% margins has no cash to invest in US-based redundancy. title: Who Holds the Purse
dek: Insurers are regaining pricing power through premiums and audits, while Medicare Advantage collapses and squeezed providers have nowhere to go.
lede: The insurers hold the purse in American healthcare. They decide how much to charge, what to cover, and how much to pay doctors and hospitals. In 2025-2026, they're pulling the purse tighter than it's been in 15 years—raising premiums aggressively, auditing providers, and exiting markets that don't make money. But the higher they raise premiums, the less room they have to negotiate, and the more providers fight back.
what_changed:
The big shift is this: for years, health insurers had thin margins and rising medical costs. Employers and patients paid more every year, but doctors and hospitals kept demanding higher fees. Starting in 2023-2024, that broke. Medical cost inflation squeezed insurer margins so hard that in 2025-2026, they stopped negotiating and started dictating. Employer-sponsored premiums rose 9% for 2026—the highest jump in 15 years. ACA marketplace premiums jumped 18%, with benchmark plans jumping 26%. Most dramatically, enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, meaning unsubsidized individual premiums flipped from $888 to $1,904 annually—more than double overnight. That's not a gradual pinch; that's a market shock. But here's the rub: premiums rose while actual medical costs rose faster. Earned premiums grew 14.3% in 2025, but incurred claims grew 15.5%—insurers are losing money on individual policies even after those steep hikes.

Medicare Advantage is the canary in the coal mine. MA is supposed to be the profit engine—insurers get a capitated per-member fee and pocket the savings if they keep people healthy. Except they can't. In 2025, for the first time in two decades, MA enrollment fell. CMS expected it to drop from 35 million in 2024 to 34 million in 2025, and 2.9 million seniors were forced to switch plans because insurers simply exited unprofitable markets. Meanwhile, the costs were killing them. In 2023, 17% of MA contracts ran above 100% medical loss ratio (MLR), meaning insurers paid out more in claims than they collected in premiums. Another third sit in the 90-95% range with no cushion at all. GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic became surprise costs that no pricing model anticipated. So CMS, facing MA's collapse and its own budget pressure, launched aggressive audits starting May 2025, targeting "upcoding"—where providers report patients as sicker than they are to justify higher risk-adjusted payments. For the first time, CMS is auditing at scale and fast-tracking cases. The threat of clawbacks forces MA plans to tighten networks, cut benefits, and demand deeper discounts from providers.

This is what payer power looks like in practice. Dental insurance shows the same pattern at smaller scale. Plan maximums haven't budged since the 1980s—still $1,000 to $1,500 annually—meaning they're worth 1/17th their 1975 purchasing power. Dentists refuse to take those networks at those reimbursement rates. Network participation collapsed to just 32% by 2024 in major PPO networks. Insurers can't deliver the care their customers paid for. So they're raising premiums and shrinking benefits. Seventeen states passed dental insurance reform laws in 2025, and 30+ more followed in 2026, mandating minimum dental loss ratios, human review of AI claim denials, and bans on retroactive coverage denials. The insurers have less room to maneuver every month.

What makes scarcest right now is provider capacity at any price. Medicaid enrollment is shrinking for the first time since COVID—down 7.6% in 2025 due to new work and reporting requirements. Employers are defecting from group dental, down 2.3% in 2024-2025. And the unsubsidized individual market is about to crater when subsidies expire. Insurers need to raise premiums to cover rising medical costs, but raising premiums drives people out of insurance altogether, especially in the individual market. Volume is collapsing just as costs rise. Tariffs from the Trump administration added 2-3.6% to premium bills across device and supply costs, making it worse. Meanwhile, new entrants like Amazon—now offering GLP-1 drugs at $25/month through One Medical and same-day pharmacy delivery in 3,000 cities by mid-2026—are siphoning the most profitable segments. TrumpRx.gov, launched in February 2026 with GoodRx integration, lets patients buy drugs at manufacturer-discounted cash prices without insurance altogether. Insurers are losing pricing power over drugs even as they're trying to exercise it over providers.

Dental service organizations (DSOs) are consolidating practices faster than ever (16.1% by 2024, up from 7.2% in 2015), concentrating supply-side bargaining power and reducing insurers' leverage—when one practice is worth negotiating with, insurers have to negotiate. Patients on employer plans with subsidies win by locking in coverage before unsubsidized premiums double. And new entrants like Amazon, bypassing insurance entirely with cash prices, are winning the marginal customer who can't afford premiums.
lose: Providers lose hardest. Doctors and hospitals see MA network exits force them to renegotiate at lower rates or lose entire patient populations. Dentists watch network participation collapse as insurers refuse to pay, then get accused of leaving networks when they exit. Solo practices and small group practices can't absorb margin compression and are consolidating into DSOs or going cash-only. Patients in the individual ACA market lose access when subsidies expire—enrollment will crater when unsubsidized premiums double. Regional MA plans like Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare ceased all operations except MA by January 2026, abandoning hundreds of thousands of Medicaid and ACA enrollees. Medicaid beneficiaries lose most acutely: enrollment is shrinking for the first time since COVID, and states are cutting faster than CMS anticipated.
worry: The single biggest risk is that insurers can't actually keep raising premiums without destroying their own customer base. The individual market is one shock away from death spiral. When unsubsidized premiums double from $888 to $1,904 in 2026, enrollment will crater. Younger, healthier people will drop out, leaving only sick and older people in the pool. Claims per member will spike. Insurers will raise premiums again. More people drop out. Each cycle narrows the pool until the market doesn't exist. That's not speculation—it happened in the pre-ACA individual market in the 2000s. Meanwhile, the payer power itself is being undermined. CMS audits for upcoding and tariffs from the Trump administration are raising costs faster than premiums can follow. GLP-1 drugs cost more than anyone modeled. New entrants are siphoning profitable segments. And providers, especially consolidated DSOs and large hospital systems, are pushing back harder—consolidation means fewer players to negotiate with, and they can say no.
one_sentence: Insurers regained pricing power by raising premiums sharply in 2025-2026, but medical costs are rising faster, enrollment is collapsing, and new entrants are bypassing them entirely.

title: The independent-practice exodus
dek: Solo dentists and mental health clinics sell to networks and PE to escape the pricing squeeze.
lede: Reimbursement stagnation is forcing independent practitioners out. Dental practices that once thrived solo are now selling to DSO networks at record pace. Mental health clinics are consolidating just as fast, chasing economies of scale and digital scale that independents can't afford. The math is simple: margins compress, costs rise, and only large platforms can negotiate with payers and absorb the hit.
what_changed:
The pricing squeeze is real and measurable. In dentistry, nearly 60% of independent practitioners report that reimbursement rates have stagnated since 2021, and another 25% say rates have actually fallen. Yet patient demand is climbing—one in five Americans will be 65 or older by 2030, driving volume up. But volume doesn't matter if the price per visit keeps dropping. Dental practice margins fell from 15.3% in 2022 to 15–16% in 2026 as costs pressured profits despite higher throughput. The result is a stampede into DSO (Dental Service Organization) networks. In 2024, about 16% of dentists were DSO-affiliated. By 2026, that number nearly tripled to 39% of practices. In the first half of 2026 alone, 175-plus dental practice locations sold to DSOs and other buyers. New graduates are especially vulnerable: average dental school debt hit $297,800 in 2025, making the solo practice path financially treacherous when reimbursement is flat.

Mental health clinics face a parallel but slightly different squeeze. The market is growing at 4.8% year-over-year, and demand is real—buprenorphine prescriptions nearly tripled to 15.4 million in 2024, and overdose deaths fell from 110,000 in 2023 to about 75,000 in 2024. But reimbursement is tightening. Telehealth claim denials jumped 84% from 2024 to 2025, squeezing the revenue margin for clinics that depend on remote visits. Wages for psychiatrists and counselors are rising faster than revenue can keep up. A 2021 baseline margin of 5.8% is being compressed by wage inflation, and there's a projected shortage of 43,660 to 93,940 adult psychiatrists by 2037. The M&A boom accelerated to 104 behavioral health deals in 2025 (up from 73 in 2024), with mental health subsector accounting for over 80 of those transactions. Solo and small clinics are selling out because they can't compete on scale, technology, or digital reach.

What makes this collapse distinct from typical consolidation is that reimbursement doesn't improve much for the buyers either—they're not conquering the payers, they're just surviving better by cutting overhead, spreading fixed costs across more locations, and building the digital infrastructure payers now demand. A DSO can negotiate slightly more aggressively than a solo practice with 10 chairs, but not enough to reverse the trend. The exodus is driven by desperation, not ambition. The consolidators (PE-backed DSO platforms like Smile Doctors, which acquired myOrthos with 70-plus orthodontic practices across 13 states in 2025) and health systems don't win on price—they win on survival. They absorb the 5.8% margins in mental health and the 15–16% margins in dentistry, cross-subsidize with adjacent services, and outlast the independents.

Graduate debt policy is accelerating the shift. In July 2026, federal Grad PLUS student loans were eliminated for new dental students, and new income-driven repayment plans shifted to 1–10% income-based calculations. This reshapes the calculus: a dentist with $298,000 in debt can repay faster working inside a DSO with a guaranteed salary than betting everything on a solo practice in a reimbursement-flat market. The independence that defined the profession is now a liability, not an asset.

title: Volume up, price down
dek: Aging brings more patients, but Medicare's 82-87 cent payment per dollar of care means volume alone can't save anyone from margin collapse.
lede: The aging population is real. US hospitals, home care agencies, and device makers are seeing patient and service volume rise year after year. Medicare expanded ambulatory surgery center procedures in 2026. Home care demand grew 6.7% annually from 2021 to 2026. But here's the trap: the more you grow volume, the more you bleed on price. Medicare reimburses hospitals at only 82-87 cents per dollar of actual care cost. Home care agencies face stacked payment cuts—2026 brought a 1.3% reduction after proposing 6.4%. You can't cost-cut your way out of that math.
what_changed:
Aging was supposed to be a tailwind for healthcare providers. The US population is getting older, and older people need more care—dialysis, joint replacements, wound care, home health aides. The industry grew to 1.5 trillion dollars in 2025 and is adding 2.4 million more home care workers by 2026. But volume without price power is a trap. Medicare sets the price, and it hasn't budged off its punishing rate: hospitals get 82-87 cents back for every dollar of care they deliver, leaving a 13-18 cent shortfall per case. Meanwhile, the hospitals that provide that care face labor costs that exploded 42% since 2020. Nurses struck at Kaiser in January 2026—30,000 workers—because wages haven't kept pace. Home care agencies confront a darker version of the same squeeze: caregiver wages rose from $13.07 per hour in 2014 to $16.77 in 2024, but the agencies can't raise prices to match because Medicare cuts keep falling. The industry absorbed a 1.3% payment cut in 2026 alone, on top of four straight years of cuts. No amount of volume compensates for that gap.

The math is forcing consolidation and collapse. Hospitals went from 7.6% margins in 2022 to just 1-2% by 2025—a structural profitability crisis. Hospital M&A fell to 46 deals in 2025, the lowest in 15 years, but rebounded sharply in Q1 2026 with 22 transactions worth 14.5 billion dollars as survivors went hunting for scale. Twenty healthcare bankruptcies hit in 2025, the highest count in years; Steward Health Care became the largest hospital-sector bankruptcy in 30 years, and Prospect Medical Holdings shed 10 of its 16 hospitals. Home care is worse: 34% of agencies reported profit concerns in 2025-2026, and many run at near-zero or negative margins. The industry is fracturing. Rural and underserved home care agencies are closing outright. Consolidation is aggressive: General Atlantic bought TEAM Services Group for 3 billion dollars in Q2 2026, the largest home care deal on record. Private equity now backs 41% of deal volume, betting that only platforms large enough to absorb the payment cuts and labor inflation will survive.

What's particularly brutal is that the volume growth is real but doesn't help individual providers. Ambulatory surgery centers—which don't carry hospital overhead—now do 9% more procedures than in 2023 and are stealing profitable work from hospitals. Hospitals know this, so they're buying ASCs themselves (Ascension's 3.9 billion dollar AmSurg deal), cannibalizing their own core business. Home care agencies report 95% of their workforce is under moderate-to-severe staffing stress and are turning away 25% of patient requests because they can't afford to staff up at current reimbursement rates. The turnover is grueling: 75% annual turnover among caregivers. Volume, in other words, is rising, but the people delivering it are leaving as fast as they're hired because the work is hard and the pay is low. Only large platforms with access to cheap capital, technology that drives automation (75% of health systems now use at least one AI tool, up from 59% in 2025), and enough scale to negotiate leverage can weather the margin collapse. Everyone else is being squeezed out of the market.

title: The value-based bet
dek: Providers and insurers are racing to move surgery and complex care out of hospitals and into cheaper sites — but reimbursement lags behind the costs of making it work.
one_sentence: When price-per-unit falls, the only escape is to squeeze costs by moving procedures to cheaper venues like ambulatory surgery centers — a bet that only scaled operators can win.
lede: Hospitals and insurers know they're losing money on every claim. The fix they're betting on: move surgeries and procedures out of expensive inpatient settings into cheaper ambulatory surgery centers, urgent care, and home-based models. Reimbursement is low. Labor is scarce. But if you can run at massive scale, the math might work.
what_changed:
The $46.5 billion US ambulatory surgery center market is the proving ground for this gamble. Hospitals and private equity are buying up independent ASCs at a frantic pace—Ascension Health paid $3.9 billion for AmSurg in 2024, expanding from 58 to over 300 ASCs across 34 states in a single swallow. Surgery Partners shed hospital assets (selling two Idaho hospitals for $1.15 billion to Intermountain in 2025), signaling a hard pivot: surgeries belong at ASCs, not hospital outpatient departments, because the site-of-service payment gap is real money.

The problem is reimbursement growth does not keep up with reality. CMS added 560 new procedures to the ASC Covered Procedures List in 2026—cardiac ablations, lumbar fusion, complex spine work that used to live in hospitals. But the payment rates for those procedures at ASCs are thinner than in hospital outpatient settings, by design. Meanwhile, wage inflation and operational costs have not slowed. Large platforms like United Surgical Partners (USPI) still hit 38.6% EBITDA margins in 2025, but smaller independents have been compressed into the low-to-mid 30s. Anesthesia shortages are acute—locum tenens use jumped 17% since 2024 and is projected to climb another 5% in 2026. Nursing shortages are equally severe, as hospitals and ASCs bid against each other for the same scarce staff.

The result is hard polarization. Scaled platforms—Ascension, Cleveland Clinic (via Regent Surgical), General Atlantic (via the National Platform acquisition of Legent Health in October 2025)—can absorb margin pressure because they negotiate at volume and spread overhead across hundreds of centers. They can also absorb the compliance burden. A solo or small-group ASC cannot. The value-based escape hatch works only if you run enough volume to drop the per-unit cost below what a hospital can achieve. That math is physics: if CMS pays the same rate for a cardiac ablation at an ASC as at a hospital outpatient department, but the ASC has half the overhead, the ASC wins on margin. But if the ASC has to pay locum anesthesia at $3,000 a day because staff is scarce, and the hospital outpatient department has staff on salary, the hospital wins. Scale determines which side of that crossover you land on.

The HMO side reinforces the pressure. Medical loss ratios (MLRs) are in crisis: 17% of Medicare Advantage contracts ran above 100% MLR in 2023, and another third sit in the 90–95% range with no cushion. Earned premiums rose 14.3% in 2025, but incurred claims grew 15.5%—meaning insurers are losing money on the policies themselves. GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic are surprise costs that no model predicted. CMS is auditing upcoding aggressively (May 2025 directive). And the aging population is not choosing cheaper sites—it is arriving sick and complex. So the only lever left is to steer volume away from expensive venues. Medicare Advantage enrollment itself contracted for the first time in two decades, falling from 35 million in 2024 to around 34 million in 2025, with as many as 2.9 million seniors forced to switch plans because insurers exited unprofitable markets. By January 2026, regional insurers like Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare had ceased all operations except Medicare Advantage itself—a kind of death spiral where the only line of business left is the one losing the most money.

title: The Pricing-Power Collapse
dek: Medicare cuts and payer power strip pricing from providers and device makers — volume rises with aging, but the price per unit keeps falling, and only scale survives.
lede: Healthcare reimbursement is locked in a squeeze. Medicare cuts rates by 1–2% yearly while demand grows 3–4%, so you need to see more patients just to stay flat. Payers control the price, and only the biggest operators can absorb the margin compression.
what_changed:
The pricing-power collapse across healthcare has made volume abundant but price per unit scarce. Start with dialysis: the US industry treats 516,837 patients on dialysis in 2025, generating $36 billion in revenue at just 11.7% operating margin—and Medicare rate increases are running at 2.2% for 2026 and only 1.1% projected for 2027, far below wage inflation and labor costs. Fresenius and DaVita are both growing treatment volume 2–3% annually, but revenue-per-treatment is falling in their commercial mix, and CMS's final 2027 ESRD PPS base rate of $299.55 per treatment—a $17.84 increase—translates to only 1.1% total growth after phosphate binder bundling. The message is ruthless: you need more patients, not higher prices.

Orthopedic device makers face the same pressure inverted. Medicare reimbursement for hip replacements has fallen 39% since 2017, and all orthopedic procedures saw a 26% cut from 2016 to 2024, with CMS applying a fresh 2.5% efficiency adjustment in 2026. Yet the aging US population—10,000 Americans turning 65 daily, with 37% of diagnostic tests and 34% of inpatient procedures now driven by the over-65 crowd—still drives steady demand. Stryker captured 67% of US knee procedures on its MAKO robotic platform by year-end 2025, proving that robotic surgery (a $2.6 billion market growing 16–17% annually) is the only escape hatch from commodity pricing. The orthopedic industry margins compressed to 5.6% as of 2022, and consolidation is accelerating: J&J is spinning off DePuy Synthes (valued $20 billion+) precisely because the orthopedic business can't compete at scale against focused players.

Generic pharma is broken. The market contracted from $40.6 billion in 2022 to $28.5 billion in 2026—a -10% CAGR over five years—as PBMs took 80% control of the market and set prices to near-commodity levels. Teva reported 15% US generics growth in 2024 but issued subdued 2025 guidance under ongoing pricing pressure and patent cliffs. India and China now supply 58% of US pharmaceutical imports by weight, with India shipping $10.5 billion annually while depending on China for 70% of raw materials. Congress's February 2026 legislation delinking PBM compensation from drug prices is the most significant regulatory intervention in decades, but it won't raise manufacturer prices—it just shifts the PBM's profit model and leaves makers facing tariff threats (100% tariffs on generic drugs threatened by August 2028) and the race to biosimilars. Generic manufacturers with 5–15% margins are forced to exit the commodity business entirely and pivot to complex molecules and biosimilars (20–40% margins) to survive.

Finally, insurers are the one sector that just recaptured pricing power. After medical cost inflation crushed margins in 2023–2024, the Big Three (UnitedHealth, Humana, CVS/Aetna) are hiking premiums aggressively in 2025–2026: employer-sponsored premiums are rising 9%—the highest in 15 years—while ACA marketplace premiums jumped 18% for 2026, and benchmark plans jumped 26%. The expiration of enhanced ACA subsidies on December 31, 2025 means unsubsidized individual premiums will more than double from $888 to $1,904 annually. Medicaid shrinkage—down 7.6% in 2025 and growing only 0.2% in 2026 due to new work/reporting requirements—lets insurers shed the lowest-margin segment. But that power is temporary and defensive: tariff pressures are raising device and supply costs, Medicaid enrollment is evaporating, and new entrants like Amazon (which launched a GLP-1 management program in April 2026 at $25/month in ~3,000 cities) and TrumpRx.gov (a direct-to-consumer pharmacy that launched February 2026) are siphoning off the most profitable segments—employee health, primary care, and specialty drugs.

Made scarce: pricing power over units and premium growth. Made cheap: individual insurance coverage for the unsubsidized (due to subsidy cliffs), generic drugs (PBM leverage), and outpatient procedures (site-neutral payment rules). Made risky: being a small operator without scale or being locked into low-margin commodity products. Made valuable: being a consolidator with scale (dialysis giants DaVita and Fresenius), owning proprietary innovation (Stryker in robotic surgery), and being an insurer with enough enrollment to absorb margin compression through premium hikes.
